subject: Physics
scope_summary: Grade-10 reflection and spherical-mirror self-study spine: normal-referenced reflection, real/virtual image geometry, Cartesian optical signs, spherical-mirror principal-ray construction, signed mirror equation and signed magnification. Refraction/lenses and later optics remain outside this bounded slice.

resources.title: Track C authored reflection and image-geometry rung draft
resources.locator: Track C / reflection and mirror rung authoring
resources.section: Reflection and spherical mirrors through ray construction, mirror equation and magnification
resources.rights_status: Author-created project draft; no external reproduction rights claimed.
resources.selection_reason: Keeps the existing local optics foundations, then copies/adapts only the missing spherical-mirror semantics needed for the bounded Grade-10 mirror slice. Historical donor readiness/curriculum authority is not inherited.

buckets.title: Reflection and spherical mirrors
buckets.badge_reason: The durable difficulty is keeping reflected-ray geometry, the declared Cartesian sign convention, the paraxial mirror model and magnification orientation mutually consistent.

scope.covers: Grade-10 reflection and spherical mirrors: normal-based reflection, real/virtual image geometry, Cartesian optical signs, principal-ray image construction, signed mirror formula, signed magnification, applications and focal-length practical reasoning.
excluded: Refraction and refractive-index teaching beyond what a later bounded lens/refraction slice explicitly owns.
Spherical-lens formulae, lens power and human-eye correction.
Aberration calculations, thick-mirror models and advanced multi-element optics.

conventions.statement: Use the mirror pole as origin; declare the incident-light direction as positive longitudinal direction and upward from the principal axis as positive height before assigning signs.

capabilities.action: Construct a reflected path by measuring both ray directions from the surface normal.
capabilities.success_criterion: Draw the outgoing path with the same normal-referenced angle as the incoming path.

capabilities.action: Classify an image point from actual reflected-path intersection versus backward-extension intersection.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify real or virtual image geometry from where the light paths or their backward extensions meet.

capabilities.action: Assign signs to mirror distances and heights from a declared pole, incident-light direction and vertical convention.
capabilities.success_criterion: Give the sign of each optical coordinate by its measurement direction rather than by object or image labels.

capabilities.action: Construct and interpret a spherical-mirror image using a consistent pair of principal rays.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses valid principal-ray rules for one mirror state, locates one common physical or backward-extension intersection, and classifies the resulting image geometry without mixing incompatible ray rules.

capabilities.action: Use the signed spherical-mirror equation within its paraxial model and cross-check the predicted image with the ray construction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares the coordinate convention, uses 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for the same paraxial mirror state, preserves signs while rearranging, and rejects the equation as an exact arbitrary-wide-aperture law.

capabilities.action: Use signed mirror magnification to connect image size and orientation with signed object/image distances.
capabilities.success_criterion: Relates m = h_i/h_o = -v/u for one mirror state and interprets magnification magnitude as relative size and sign as erect/inverted orientation.

microtopics.title: Measure reflection from the normal, not the surface
microtopics.badge_reason: A familiar mirror picture becomes wrong immediately if the reference line for the angle is the surface instead of the normal.
entry_assumptions: Can trace a directed straight path and identify where it meets a surface.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Angles in specular reflection are measured from the surface normal, and the reflected ray leaves with the same angle to that normal as the incident ray.

teaching_path.action: At the point where the incoming light path meets the mirror, draw the line perpendicular to the surface before marking any angle.
teaching_path.why_valid: The reflection angle is defined relative to this perpendicular reference, so drawing it first fixes the reference instead of letting the page edge stand in for it.
teaching_path.output: mirror surface ⟂ normal at the contact point

teaching_path.action: Copy the incoming path's tilt from the normal to the opposite side of that normal to construct the outgoing path.
teaching_path.why_valid: Using the same reference line on both sides preserves the reflection rule while making the outgoing direction observable on the drawing.
teaching_path.output: incoming tilt from normal -> matching outgoing tilt on the other side

teaching_path.action: Rotate the entire drawing on the page and repeat the construction without changing the physical geometry.
teaching_path.why_valid: A page rotation changes how the paper is oriented but not perpendicularity or the pair of equal normal-referenced angles.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ray makes 20 degrees with the mirror surface. Is its angle of incidence 20 degrees?
misconceptions.repair: Draw the normal first; incidence and reflection angles are defined from that line, not from the surface.

exit_task.prompt: Given an incoming light path and a plane mirror drawn at an arbitrary page angle, construct the normal and the reflected path, and state which line the two reflection angles are measured from.

answer.summary: Draw the perpendicular normal at the contact point, then place the outgoing path on the other side with the same tilt to that normal; both angles are measured from the normal.
reasoning: Locate the point where the incoming path meets the surface.
Draw the perpendicular reference there before reading or copying any angle.
Use the same reference on the opposite side to place the outgoing path.
answer.check: Rotate the page mentally. If the construction depends on the page edge rather than the normal, it will change; a correct construction will not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is a geometric construction and reference-line explanation, not a numerical angle calculation.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created construction turns the normal-reference rule into a directed-path task suitable for review before any spherical-mirror equation is introduced.

predict.prompt: If you rotate the mirror drawing on the page but keep the physical incoming path fixed relative to it, should the reflection construction change?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The construction is tied to the surface normal at the contact point, not to the page orientation.

attempt.produces: A reflected-path construction on an oblique mirror with the normal drawn first and both angle arcs referenced to it.

rubric.criterion: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror at the contact point.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the correct reference line for both angles.

rubric.criterion: Incoming and outgoing angle marks are placed on opposite sides of the same normal.
rubric.evidence_of: Applying the reflection symmetry to a single local reference.

accepted: The drawing places one perpendicular normal at the contact point and shows matching angle marks between each path and that normal.
rejected: The angle arcs are drawn between each path and the mirror surface, so the construction uses the wrong reference even if the final path happens to look symmetric.

route.ask: At the exact contact point, which line could give both the incoming and outgoing path the same local reference?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the missing perpendicular reference before the rule is named.

route.ask: Once that line is drawn, where would you place an outgoing path with the same tilt but on the other side?
route.why_this_ask: The learner performs the geometric transformation rather than receiving the finished ray.

route.ask: If the paper is rotated, which relationships in your construction must remain unchanged?
route.why_this_ask: The page-rotation check exposes surface-based memorization.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path names the normal immediately; the elicitation route begins from the need for a common local reference and makes the learner propose the perpendicular line.

boundary_test.prompt: What happens for an incoming path that lies exactly along the normal?
boundary_test.answer: The outgoing path retraces the same line in the opposite direction because its tilt from the normal is zero on both sides.
boundary_test.confirms: The normal, rather than the surface, is the defining angular reference.

microtopics.title: Real and virtual describe how light paths meet
microtopics.badge_reason: The everyday word virtual invites a false not-recordable interpretation unless image type is tied directly to ray geometry.
entry_assumptions: R1: reflection direction is fixed by equal angles measured from the normal.
microtopics.inferential_jump: An image location is determined by where reflected rays actually meet or where their backward extensions appear to meet; virtual describes ray geometry, not whether a camera can record it.

teaching_path.action: Trace at least two reflected light paths from the same object point and keep their physical forward portions solid.
teaching_path.why_valid: One path cannot locate an image point; two or more paths reveal whether the light itself converges.
teaching_path.output: two reflected paths -> enough geometry to test a meeting point

teaching_path.action: When the reflected paths diverge, extend them backward with a visibly different line style until the extensions meet.
teaching_path.why_valid: The extensions are a geometric inference about apparent origin, not additional light travelling behind the mirror, so changing the line style preserves that distinction.
teaching_path.output: solid paths diverge -> dashed backward extensions meet behind the mirror

teaching_path.action: Place an eye or camera where it can receive the reflected bundle and ask whether collecting those diverging paths changes where their backward extensions meet.
teaching_path.why_valid: A detector can refocus incoming light without converting the mirror's apparent-origin geometry into an actual meeting point at the mirror.
teaching_path.output: camera receives reflected bundle -> apparent mirror-image location remains virtual

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A virtual image is not a usable image and therefore cannot be photographed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A camera points at a plane mirror and records your reflection. Does that make the mirror image real?
misconceptions.repair: Separate image geometry from recording: the mirror sends diverging rays that a camera lens can collect and refocus.

exit_task.prompt: Given two reflected light paths from one object point, classify the image location from whether the physical paths meet or only their backward extensions meet, and explain why visibility or photography does not change that classification.

answer.summary: An actual meeting of reflected light paths gives a real image point; a meeting only of backward extensions gives a virtual image point, and either ray bundle can still enter an eye or camera.
reasoning: Use more than one reflected path so an intersection is a geometric fact rather than an assumption.
Distinguish physical forward paths from backward extensions by line style and direction.
Classify the image from which kind of intersection occurs, not from whether a detector can receive the light.
answer.check: Remove the observer or camera from the drawing. The path intersection or backward-extension intersection that defines the image should not move.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer classifies path geometry and detector independence; it asserts no computed distance or image size.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created two-path construction gives the virtual-image misconception a geometric diagnostic without invoking later principal-ray or mirror-equation machinery.

predict.prompt: If a camera successfully records a plane-mirror image, does that prove the reflected light actually met behind the mirror?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The camera can collect diverging reflected light even though only backward extensions meet behind the mirror.

attempt.produces: A two-path diagram with physical reflected paths and backward extensions drawn differently, plus a real-or-virtual classification justified from the intersection.

rubric.criterion: Physical reflected paths and backward extensions are visually distinguished.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping actual light travel separate from apparent origin.

rubric.criterion: The image type is tied to which lines intersect, not to whether the image can be seen.
rubric.evidence_of: Using ray geometry as the classification rule.

accepted: The reflected paths are solid, their behind-mirror extensions are dashed, and the answer calls the behind-mirror point virtual because only the extensions intersect there.
rejected: The answer calls the image real solely because a camera can photograph it, without checking whether the reflected paths themselves ever meet behind the mirror.

route.ask: How many reflected paths do you need before an image location can be fixed by intersection?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents one arbitrary path from being treated as an image locator.

route.ask: If those paths spread apart, what lines could you extend backward to ask where they appear to come from?
route.why_this_ask: The learner constructs apparent origin from observed directions.

route.ask: Would putting a camera in the bundle move that apparent origin?
route.why_this_ask: It directly tests the mistaken link between recordability and image type.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path distinguishes solid paths from extensions; the elicitation route starts with the successful camera observation and forces the learner to decide whether detection changes the mirror geometry.

boundary_test.prompt: If two reflected light paths actually cross in front of a mirror before entering a detector, which classification follows from that crossing?
boundary_test.answer: That crossing is a real image point because the physical reflected paths themselves meet there.
boundary_test.confirms: Real versus virtual is determined by path intersection, independent of whether an observer is present.

microtopics.title: Optical signs come from declared directions
microtopics.badge_reason: Memorized object-and-image sign tables fail as soon as the drawing is mirrored or a less familiar optical configuration is used.
entry_assumptions: R2: image nature is determined by actual versus backward-extended ray intersection.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The Cartesian sign convention turns a mirror diagram into signed distances and heights; the signs come from declared directions, not from memorized object/image labels.

teaching_path.action: Mark the pole as the distance origin, declare the direction of incident light as the positive horizontal direction, and declare upward from the principal axis as positive height.
teaching_path.why_valid: Signs can only be reproducible when the origin and positive directions are fixed before any object or image is classified.
teaching_path.output: pole = origin; incident-light direction = positive distance; upward = positive height

teaching_path.action: Take several marked points and assign each a distance sign from the pole and a height sign from the principal axis using only the declared directions.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same coordinate rule applies to every point, so the result cannot depend on whether a point is called object, image, center or another label.
teaching_path.output: with incident direction -> positive distance; against it -> negative distance; above axis -> positive height; below -> negative height

teaching_path.action: Redraw the same physical setup reversed left-to-right on the page, carrying the declared incident-light arrow with it, and assign the signs again.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct convention follows the declared physical direction, so changing the page layout does not change the signs of the same physical quantities.
teaching_path.output: page reversed + direction declaration carried with setup -> physical sign assignments preserved

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Object distance is always negative and image distance is always positive.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Move the same object-and-mirror sketch so incident light travels the opposite page direction. Should the sign rule follow the page or the declared incident-light direction?
misconceptions.repair: Apply the coordinate convention from the pole every time; signs follow measurement direction and height orientation.

exit_task.prompt: A mirror diagram declares its pole, incident-light direction and upward direction. Assign signs to the object distance, image distance, focal-location distance and image height from those declarations, and explain why an object-or-image sign table was unnecessary.

answer.summary: Each sign follows the declared coordinate direction from the pole or principal axis; the labels object and image do not determine signs by themselves.
reasoning: Use the pole as the horizontal origin and compare every longitudinal position with the declared incident-light direction.
Use the principal axis as the vertical reference and compare each height with the declared upward direction.
Apply those two rules consistently to every named point instead of switching rules when the label changes.
answer.check: Mirror the whole drawing left-to-right while carrying the incident-light arrow with the physical setup; a convention-based answer should remain physically consistent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer assigns qualitative signs from a declared coordinate convention and computes no numerical optical result.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created sign-assignment routine makes the coordinate convention explicit before any gated mirror equation or magnification relation is used.

predict.prompt: If the same mirror setup is drawn on the opposite side of the page, should an object's sign change merely because its ink moved left or right?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The sign follows the declared incident-light and vertical directions, which move with the physical setup rather than staying attached to page left or page right.

attempt.produces: A sign-labelled mirror sketch with origin and positive directions declared before any object, image or focal-location signs are assigned.

rubric.criterion: The pole and both positive directions are declared before signs are written.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the coordinate convention as the source of the signs.

rubric.criterion: Every longitudinal and vertical sign is justified by direction from the declared reference.
rubric.evidence_of: Avoiding memorized sign rules tied to object or image labels.

accepted: The sketch marks the pole, incident-light arrow and upward direction first, then gives each position and height a sign by comparing it with those declarations.
rejected: The response writes object is negative and image is positive before declaring any direction, so the signs are attached to labels rather than coordinates.

route.ask: Before assigning any sign, where is the distance origin in this diagram?
route.why_this_ask: A sign without an origin is not a coordinate decision.

route.ask: Which physical direction has been declared positive for longitudinal distance, and which for height?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must state both coordinate directions before classifying points.

route.ask: Take one point without calling it object or image. Which sign follows from its direction from the pole?
route.why_this_ask: Removing the familiar label tests whether the coordinate rule can stand on its own.

route.ask: If the page drawing is reversed, what must move with the setup so your signs remain physically consistent?
route.why_this_ask: The reversal exposes page-left or page-right memorization.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path declares a full coordinate system first; the elicitation route removes object and image labels and makes the learner recover signs from an unlabeled point before testing a mirrored page layout.

boundary_test.prompt: What sign should a point exactly at the pole have for its longitudinal distance?
boundary_test.answer: Its distance is zero, so it is neither on the positive nor negative side of the origin.
boundary_test.confirms: The sign convention is a coordinate system with an origin, not a permanent label attached to a class of optical object.

microtopics.title: Principal rays are consistent shortcuts to one spherical-mirror image
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners can memorize individual ray rules yet combine them inconsistently or treat one ray as sufficient to locate an image.
entry_assumptions: Can classify real versus virtual intersections and assign optical signs from the declared pole/axis convention.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A small set of principal-ray rules are not independent tricks: any valid pair for the same object point and spherical mirror must locate the same image point within the model.

teaching_path.action: Label the mirror type, pole, principal axis, focus and centre of curvature, then identify whether each referenced focus/centre is physical or reached by backward extension for that mirror.
teaching_path.why_valid: Principal-ray rules depend on one declared spherical-mirror geometry; the same labels cannot be moved independently from the mirror.
teaching_path.output: one labelled spherical-mirror geometry with P, principal axis, F and C

teaching_path.action: From one object point, construct two valid principal rays: parallel-axis/focus, focus/parallel, or centre-of-curvature/retrace, using backward extensions where the convex-mirror rule requires them.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each construction is a constrained consequence of the same spherical-mirror geometry, so a valid pair determines one image point.
teaching_path.output: two consistent reflected paths or reflected paths plus backward extensions

teaching_path.action: Use a third valid principal ray as a consistency check and classify the image from actual versus backward-extension intersection, orientation and relative size.
teaching_path.why_valid: An independent third construction should agree with the image location if the first two ray rules were applied consistently.
teaching_path.output: one cross-checked image point with real/virtual and erect/inverted classification

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any two memorized principal-ray sketches can be combined even if they predict different image points.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two correctly labelled rays from the same object point and mirror predict different image locations. Can both constructions be valid?
misconceptions.repair: No. Recheck the mirror type, focus/centre side and before/after ray directions until all valid rays agree on one physical or backward-extension intersection.

exit_task.prompt: For a concave mirror with the object beyond the centre of curvature, describe two principal rays from the top of the object and use their meeting to state the image region and whether the image is real or virtual and erect or inverted.

answer.summary: A parallel ray reflects through the focus and a ray through the centre of curvature retraces its path; they meet in front of the mirror between F and C, giving a real inverted image.
reasoning: Both rays belong to the same concave-mirror geometry.
The physical reflected rays meet in front of the mirror, so the image is real.
Their intersection lies below the principal axis for an upright object, so the image is inverted.
answer.check: A third ray directed through the focus should reflect parallel to the axis and pass through the same image point.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit verifies qualitative ray geometry, image region and image nature; it asserts no computed distance or magnification.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copies/adapts durable spherical-mirror ray-construction invariants from prior internal Physics engineering while retaining the existing Grade9V3 coordinate/image foundations and current Grade-10 scope.

predict.prompt: If you use two different valid principal-ray pairs for the same object point and spherical mirror, may they legitimately locate two different images?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Within the model, every valid pair must locate the same image point or the same backward-extension point.

attempt.produces: A labelled spherical-mirror diagram with two independently chosen principal rays and an image classification justified from their intersection.

rubric.criterion: Both rays obey valid before/after directions for the declared mirror geometry.
rubric.evidence_of: Using geometry rather than decorative memorized lines.

rubric.criterion: The image classification follows physical versus backward-extension intersection and orientation.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting the construction to image nature.

accepted: Two valid rays meet at one point and the answer classifies that point from the actual reflected paths or their backward extensions.
rejected: The two rays predict different image points but the response keeps both without resolving the inconsistency.

route.ask: What mirror points must be fixed before you choose a principal ray?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents ray rules from floating independently of the mirror geometry.

route.ask: If one ray is parallel to the principal axis, where must its reflected path go for this mirror?
route.why_this_ask: It forces one concrete principal-ray decision.

route.ask: Which second ray can independently locate the same image point?
route.why_this_ask: One ray gives a direction, not an image location.

route.ask: Do the physical rays meet, or only their backward extensions?
route.why_this_ask: That distinction determines image nature.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the labelled geometry first; the learner route starts by needing a second independent locator and reconstructs why two rays, not a memorized finished diagram, define the image.

boundary_test.prompt: For a convex mirror, reflected rays diverge in front of the mirror. If their backward extensions meet behind it, is the image real or virtual?
boundary_test.answer: Virtual, because only backward extensions meet behind the mirror; the physical reflected rays do not converge there.
boundary_test.confirms: Image classification still comes from path geometry when the focus and image are virtual.

microtopics.title: The mirror equation is a signed paraxial model of the ray geometry
microtopics.badge_reason: Correct algebra can still represent the wrong physical mirror if signs are assigned from labels or if the paraxial model condition is forgotten.
entry_assumptions: Can construct a spherical-mirror image with principal rays and apply the declared Cartesian sign convention.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f does not replace the ray picture: signed u, v and f must refer to the same mirror geometry and the formula is used only within the paraxial/small-angle model.

teaching_path.action: Before substitution, mark the pole/origin and positive longitudinal direction, then assign signed u and f from the diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-EQUATION relates signed coordinates, so signs must come from the declared coordinate system rather than memorized object/image labels.
teaching_path.output: one mirror diagram with signed u and f

teaching_path.action: Use 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and rearrange it to the requested unknown without discarding signs.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-EQUATION owns the algebraic relation for the same paraxial mirror state.

teaching_path.action: Compare the sign/region predicted for v with the principal-ray construction and state the paraxial/small-angle condition behind the equation.
teaching_path.why_valid: A sign or region disagreement reveals a coordinate/construction error, while wide-aperture disagreement can reveal a model-limit issue.
teaching_path.output: equation prediction and ray construction agree within the stated model

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The mirror formula is an exact law for every ray on any part of a spherical mirror, so ray height and aperture never matter.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If rays strike far from the principal axis at large angles and fail to meet at one point, must the algebra be wrong?
misconceptions.repair: Not necessarily. State the paraxial/small-angle approximation before using the simple mirror equation; wide-aperture disagreement can be a model-limit effect.

exit_task.prompt: A concave-mirror diagram uses the declared Cartesian convention with a real object and real image in front of the mirror, so u < 0 and the ray construction says v < 0. Write the mirror equation rearranged for 1/v, state the sign you expect for v, and name the model condition that must be satisfied before trusting the equation.

answer.summary: Use 1/v = 1/f - 1/u; the physical ray construction requires v to be negative in this convention, and the spherical-mirror equation is used in the paraxial/small-angle regime.
reasoning: Keep the signs attached to u and f when rearranging.
Use the ray construction as an independent sign/region check on v.
State the paraxial model boundary rather than treating the formula as exact for arbitrary wide-aperture rays.
answer.check: If the algebra predicts an image region inconsistent with two valid principal rays, revisit signs/model use before accepting the result.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit checks symbolic rearrangement, sign consistency and model validity; no numerical image distance is asserted.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor mirror-formula model condition and falsifier into the local Grade9V3 teaching/verification contract without importing donor readiness or requiring a formula derivation that current Grade-10 scope does not demand.

predict.prompt: If a correctly drawn concave-mirror image is real and lies in front of the mirror, can a positive v from your algebra be accepted without rechecking anything?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Under the declared convention a real image in front has negative v, so the sign disagreement is evidence to recheck the setup or algebra.

attempt.produces: A sign-declared mirror-equation setup, symbolic rearrangement for the unknown, ray-diagram cross-check and explicit model-condition statement.

rubric.criterion: Signs are assigned from the declared coordinate system before substitution.
The equation result is checked against ray geometry and the paraxial model boundary is stated.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating equation and construction as one bounded physical model.

accepted: The response preserves signed u/f, solves symbolically for v, checks v's region against the ray diagram and names the paraxial condition.
rejected: The response inserts unsigned distances into the formula and treats any numerical result as valid without a ray or model check.

route.ask: Before writing the formula, what fixes the signs of u and f?
route.why_this_ask: The coordinate system must precede the algebra.

route.ask: What relation links u, v and f for this spherical-mirror model?
route.why_this_ask: It selects the governing relation rather than a lens formula.

route.ask: What image region should the principal rays predict before you trust v?
route.why_this_ask: It creates an independent physical cross-check.

route.ask: What assumption about the rays lets the simple spherical-mirror equation represent the geometry?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes the model boundary.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path moves from declared signs to algebra; the learner route starts from an expected image region and uses that physical prediction to reconstruct which signs and model condition the algebra must respect.

boundary_test.prompt: If the mirror aperture is made very wide and the relevant rays strike far from the principal axis at large angles, is failure of one-point convergence automatically an arithmetic error?
boundary_test.answer: No. It can be failure of the paraxial approximation; the simple mirror equation is not being used inside its intended small-angle model.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner distinguishes algebraic failure from model-validity failure.

microtopics.title: Signed magnification carries image size and orientation
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often keep only the absolute size ratio and lose the orientation information carried by the sign.
entry_assumptions: Can obtain signed u and v for one spherical-mirror state and classify the image from its ray construction.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Mirror magnification is not merely 'times bigger': m = h_i/h_o = -v/u is signed, so |m| gives relative size while the sign records erect versus inverted orientation under the declared convention.

teaching_path.action: Keep signed u, v, object height h_o and image height h_i tied to the same declared mirror coordinates.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-MAGNIFICATION compares quantities from one object-image state; mixing states or dropping height direction breaks its meaning.
teaching_path.output: one signed object-image state with u, v, h_o and h_i

teaching_path.action: Use m = -v/u = h_i/h_o and preserve the sign while comparing image and object size.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-MAGNIFICATION binds the distance ratio and height ratio for the same spherical-mirror image.
teaching_path.output: m = -v/u = h_i/h_o; |m| gives the image/object size ratio while sign(m) is retained for orientation.

teaching_path.action: Predict erect/inverted and enlarged/same-size/diminished from m, then check those claims against the ray diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: The ray geometry independently shows orientation and approximate relative size, so it can falsify a dropped or reversed sign.
teaching_path.output: magnification sign/size agrees with the ray construction

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Magnification is only a positive size factor, so taking |m| loses nothing important.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two images have the same absolute size ratio, but one is erect and one inverted. Can one unsigned magnification distinguish them?
misconceptions.repair: No. Preserve the sign: |m| describes relative size while the sign carries orientation under the declared convention.

exit_task.prompt: For a real object with u < 0, a principal-ray diagram shows a real inverted image in front of the mirror, so v < 0. Without using numbers, determine the sign of m = -v/u and state what that sign says about orientation.

answer.summary: m is negative, which is consistent with an inverted image.
reasoning: With u < 0 and v < 0, v/u is positive.
The leading minus sign makes m negative.
Negative signed magnification corresponds to inversion under this convention.
answer.check: The ray diagram should also show the image below the principal axis for an upright object.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit checks only the sign and physical interpretation of magnification; no computed magnitude is asserted.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor magnification-sign invariant into the local Grade10 mirror spine and keeps orientation as part of the learner capability instead of reducing magnification to an unsigned arithmetic ratio.

predict.prompt: If two mirror images are equally large but one is erect and the other inverted, can they have the same signed magnification?
predict.defensible_answer: No. They can have the same magnitude |m| but opposite signs because the sign carries orientation.

attempt.produces: A signed magnification statement connecting -v/u with h_i/h_o and a ray-diagram prediction of size and orientation.

rubric.criterion: The response preserves the sign of m and interprets |m| separately.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping orientation and relative size as distinct information.

rubric.criterion: The predicted orientation agrees with the ray construction.

accepted: The response reports negative m for an inverted image and separately interprets whether |m| is greater than, equal to or less than one.
rejected: The response replaces m with |m| immediately and cannot distinguish erect from inverted images.

route.ask: What does the ray diagram already tell you about the image orientation?
route.why_this_ask: It creates a physical target before the ratio is manipulated.

route.ask: Which signed distance ratio connects that image to the object?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the -v/u form rather than an unsigned scale factor.

route.ask: What information is carried by the sign, and what is carried by |m|?
route.why_this_ask: It separates orientation from relative size.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path introduces the signed relation and then interprets it; the learner route starts from visible image orientation and reconstructs why an unsigned ratio is insufficient.

boundary_test.prompt: If m = -1 for a spherical-mirror image, what two separate claims follow about size and orientation?
boundary_test.answer: The image has the same size as the object because |m| = 1, and it is inverted because m is negative.
boundary_test.confirms: Magnitude and sign of magnification carry different physical information.

relations.meaning: For one spherical mirror in the paraxial model, signed image distance and object distance combine to the reciprocal signed focal length.

symbols.meaning: Signed object distance measured from the mirror pole
Signed image distance measured from the mirror pole
Signed focal length of the spherical mirror

conditions: u, v and f use the same declared Cartesian sign convention and mirror pole as origin.
The spherical-mirror construction is used in the paraxial/small-angle regime.
u, v and f describe the same mirror and object-image state.

derivation.action: Take 1/v + 1/u = 1/f as the governed Grade-10 mirror relation; no formula derivation is required in this teaching slice.
derivation.why_valid: The current Grade-10 scope requires use of the mirror formula while explicitly not requiring its derivation.

derivation.action: Rearrange algebraically for the requested signed unknown while preserving the declared signs.
derivation.why_valid: Algebraic isolation does not change the governed relation.

limits: This simple spherical-mirror relation is a paraxial/small-angle model rather than an exact arbitrary-wide-aperture ray law.
The relation does not cover spherical lenses, multi-element optics or thick optical systems.
checks: u, v and f have the same length dimension.
The sign/region predicted for v agrees with a valid principal-ray construction.
The coordinate convention is declared before numerical substitution.

relations.meaning: For the same spherical-mirror image, transverse magnification is the signed image-to-object height ratio and equals negative signed image distance divided by signed object distance.

symbols.meaning: Signed object distance from the mirror pole
Signed image distance from the mirror pole
Signed image height relative to the principal axis
Signed object height relative to the principal axis

conditions: u, v, h_i and h_o use one declared Cartesian sign convention.
Object and image refer to the same spherical-mirror state.
h_o is nonzero when the height ratio is evaluated.

derivation.action: Use m = -v/u = h_i/h_o for the same signed object-image state.
derivation.why_valid: The governed relation binds distance and transverse-height ratios for one spherical-mirror image.

derivation.action: Separate the interpretation of |m| from the interpretation of the sign of m.
derivation.why_valid: Magnitude gives relative size while sign carries orientation under the declared convention.

limits: Magnification describes the same object-image state and does not by itself establish brightness or image quality.
The relation does not authorize lens magnification or multi-element optical systems.
checks: m is dimensionless because both ratios compare like dimensions.
The sign of m agrees with erect/inverted orientation in the ray diagram.
The magnitude |m| agrees qualitatively with enlarged, same-size or diminished ray geometry.

teaching_routes.title: Reveal Grade-10 reflection and spherical-mirror spine
entry_needs: Learners can trace directed paths and read simple coordinate directions.
learner_actions: Apply the declared Cartesian sign convention.
Construct a spherical-mirror image with a consistent principal-ray pair.
Use the signed mirror equation inside its paraxial model.
Interpret signed magnification as size plus orientation.
help_plan: Draw the normal before angle language.
Keep physical paths distinct from backward extensions.
Declare origin and positive directions before assigning signs.
Use a second and then third principal ray to expose an inconsistent construction.
Cross-check the signed mirror-equation prediction against the ray diagram.
Keep magnification sign separate from its absolute size factor.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: The declarative route exposes the complete reflection-to-magnification construction, including coordinate and model-validity checks.

source_preferences.reason: The local adapted source exposes all six mirror rungs with coordinate, ray, equation and magnification checks.

when_not_suitable: Do not expand this route into refraction, spherical lenses, human-eye correction, dispersion/scattering or advanced aberration calculations.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit Grade-10 reflection and spherical-mirror spine
entry_needs: Learners can commit to a path, image-type or sign decision before seeing the completed construction.
learner_actions: Invent the common angular reference at a mirror.
Infer apparent origin from two reflected paths.
Recover signs from declared directions without object-or-image mnemonics.
Reconstruct why two independent principal rays must locate one image.
Recover the signed mirror-equation setup from the physical image region and model condition.
Recover why magnification sign is required for orientation.
help_plan: Ask for the local reference line before naming the normal.
Use a camera counterexample before revealing the virtual-image repair.
Remove familiar labels before asking for signs.
Ask what a second ray contributes before showing a finished ray diagram.
Ask what sign/region the ray picture predicts before accepting mirror-formula algebra.
Ask whether an unsigned size ratio can distinguish erect from inverted images.
